promptText: Given `#cta { color: red; }`, `.link { color: blue; }`, and `a { color: black; }` all targeting `<a class="link" id="cta">`, which rule wins and why?
options: #cta wins, because ID selectors outrank class selectors in the specificity tuple regardless of source order
.link wins, because it was likely declared closer to the element in the stylesheet
a wins, because element selectors are evaluated last and override earlier declarations
All three apply simultaneously, blending to a mixed color since none uses !important
explanation: Specificity is compared as a tuple (inline, IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements) from left to right; an ID selector's component is compared before classes are even considered, so #cta (0,1,0,0) beats .link (0,0,1,0) regardless of where each rule appears in the source.

promptText: With the default `box-sizing: content-box`, an element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px`, and `border: 2px`. What is its actual rendered width?
options: 244px, because content-box's width applies only to the content area, with padding and border added on top
200px, because width always represents the final rendered box regardless of box-sizing
222px, because only the border is added to the declared width, not the padding
180px, because padding is subtracted from the declared width by default
explanation: content-box treats `width` as the content box only; padding (20px each side = 40px) and border (2px each side = 4px) are added on top, giving 200 + 40 + 4 = 244px -- the classic surprise that leads most codebases to set `box-sizing: border-box` globally.

promptText: A modal has `position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0;` but instead of anchoring to the viewport corner, it anchors to a parent element much further up the page. What is the most likely cause?
options: Some ancestor between the modal and the viewport has `position` set to something other than `static` (e.g. relative), making it the positioning context absolute looks for
Absolute positioning always anchors to the nearest scrollable ancestor, never the viewport
The modal needs `position: fixed` instead, since absolute elements can never anchor to the viewport
The parent's `z-index` value is higher than the modal's, forcing the anchor to shift
explanation: An absolutely positioned element is placed relative to the nearest ancestor whose `position` is not `static`; if an ancestor further up the tree happens to have `position: relative` (often set for an unrelated reason), it becomes the anchor instead of the viewport.

promptText: Inside a flex container with `flex-direction: column`, a developer is confused that `justify-content: center` is now centering items vertically instead of horizontally. What explains this?
options: justify-content always aligns along the main axis, and changing flex-direction to column swaps the main axis from horizontal to vertical
justify-content only works with flex-direction: row; the observed centering must be caused by align-items instead
Flex containers ignore justify-content entirely when nested inside another flex container
column direction disables justify-content and silently falls back to align-content
explanation: justify-content distributes items along the main axis, and the main axis is defined by flex-direction -- row makes it horizontal, column makes it vertical, which is exactly why switching direction appears to 'swap' which property controls which visual axis.

promptText: A developer sets `z-index: 9999` on a modal, but it still renders behind the page header. The header has no z-index but its parent has `transform: translateZ(0)`. What is the likely cause?
options: The transform on the header's parent creates a new stacking context, so the header's whole subtree stacks as a unit relative to the modal, and the modal's high z-index only matters within its own stacking context
z-index values above 999 are ignored by browsers as a safety limit
transform properties disable z-index entirely for all descendants
The modal needs `position: fixed` because z-index has no effect on absolutely positioned elements
explanation: Properties like transform, opacity < 1, filter, and will-change create a new stacking context. Once formed, z-index values inside that context are only compared against siblings within it -- a high z-index elsewhere can never reach inside or escape another context, which is why portaling the modal to the document root is the usual fix.

promptText: Why do most modern accessibility guidelines recommend using `rem` rather than `px` for font sizes across a React application?
options: rem is relative to the root element's font-size, so if a user increases their browser's default font size for readability, the whole UI scales proportionally; px is a fixed unit that ignores that user preference
px causes layout thrashing on every render, while rem is computed only once at build time
rem values are required by the CSS specification for any text inside a React component
px units are deprecated in modern CSS and will stop being supported in future browser versions
explanation: rem is relative to the root (html) element's font-size, so a user's browser-level font-size preference scales every rem-based value proportionally; px is absolute and stays frozen at the author's chosen size regardless of the user's accessibility settings.

promptText: A team wants to build a design system where changing the brand color from blue to green requires editing exactly one place, not hundreds of component files. What token architecture achieves this?
options: A semantic token layer (e.g. --color-accent) that maps to primitive tokens (e.g. --blue-500), with components consuming only the semantic layer -- remapping the semantic-to-primitive mapping changes the brand everywhere at once
Hard-coding the hex value directly in every component that needs the brand color, then using a global find-and-replace tool when it changes
Defining the color as a Sass variable, since Sass variables can be reassigned at runtime without a rebuild
Storing the color in component state and passing it down through props from the root App component
explanation: A three-tier token system (primitive -> semantic -> component) decouples intent from value: components reference semantic tokens like --color-accent, so remapping which primitive value that semantic token points to changes the brand color everywhere in one edit, instead of touching every consuming file.

promptText: Why are CSS custom properties (`--color-accent`) fundamentally better suited to runtime, per-tenant white-label theming than Sass variables (`$color-accent`)?
options: Sass variables are substituted with literal values at compile time and cease to exist in the shipped CSS, while custom properties are live values in the cascade that can be overridden per-scope and changed after the page has already loaded, with no rebuild
Sass variables can only hold numeric values, while custom properties can hold any CSS value including colors
Custom properties are faster to parse than Sass variables because they use native browser syntax
Sass variables require a separate build step for every browser, while custom properties work identically across all browsers without compilation
explanation: A Sass variable is a preprocessing-time text substitution -- by the time CSS reaches the browser it's gone, baked into literal values. A CSS custom property is a genuine runtime feature of the cascade, so setting it on document.documentElement (or per request server-side) instantly re-cascades every var() reference with no rebuild, which is exactly what per-tenant theming needs.

promptText: A single-page card component looks fine in a wide main content column but needs a more compact layout when placed in a narrow sidebar -- on the exact same viewport width. Which CSS feature solves this correctly, and why can a media query not?
options: Container queries, because they let an element query the size of its nearest ancestor container rather than the viewport; a media query only knows the viewport width, which is identical in both placements
Media queries, using a very specific pixel breakpoint tuned to the sidebar's exact width
Flexbox's flex-shrink property alone, since it automatically detects available space independent of any query mechanism
CSS Grid's auto-fit keyword, which inherently adapts any component regardless of its container context
explanation: Media queries only have access to viewport dimensions, so a card in a narrow sidebar and the same card in a wide column look identical to a media query on the same screen. Container queries (container-type + @container) let a component query its actual ancestor container's size, making it genuinely reusable across different layout contexts.

promptText: A `styled.div` component interpolates a per-item chart color directly into its template: `` background: ${p => p.color}; `` and is used to render thousands of uniquely-colored data points. What is the performance problem, and what is the standard fix?
options: Each distinct color value generates and injects a brand-new CSS class, so an unbounded number of unique colors causes an unbounded number of style injections; the fix is to pass the color through a CSS custom property via the inline style attribute while keeping the styled template static
styled-components caches all possible color values automatically, so there is no actual performance problem to fix
The fix is to switch the color prop to a CSS class name instead of a hex value, since class names are always cheaper than inline styles
The problem is that styled-components cannot accept dynamic props at all, so the color must be hard-coded per component instance
explanation: Runtime CSS-in-JS generates and injects a new class for every distinct resolved style string; a continuously-variable prop like a per-item color produces effectively unbounded unique classes. Routing the value through a CSS variable set via the style attribute keeps the generated CSS rule static while the browser's own cascade handles per-element value substitution for free.

promptText: Why does styled-components have friction inside React Server Components, while CSS Modules and Tailwind do not?
options: styled-components relies on React context (ThemeProvider) and runtime style injection, which requires a client boundary ("use client"), pulling more JS to the client; CSS Modules and Tailwind resolve to static class names and .css files a Server Component can reference with no client-side dependency
React Server Components technically cannot render any <div> that has a className attribute at all
CSS Modules and Tailwind are newer technologies that were designed specifically to replace React Server Components
styled-components stopped supporting server-side rendering entirely as of React 18
explanation: Runtime CSS-in-JS needs JavaScript execution (context providers, hashing, style injection) to produce its output, which requires opting into a client boundary and conflicts with keeping a subtree as pure, JS-free server-rendered markup -- exactly the goal RSC is designed around. Build-time solutions produce plain static output with no such requirement.

promptText: Two Tailwind utility classes for the same CSS property are concatenated on one element: a base `p-4` from a component and an override `p-2` passed in via a consumer's className prop. Naive string concatenation sometimes leaves the wrong padding applied. Why, and what tool fixes it?
options: Both classes are valid, non-conflicting-by-name utility classes, so whichever one happens to be declared later in Tailwind's generated stylesheet wins, regardless of which one was intended to override; tailwind-merge resolves this by understanding Tailwind's utility semantics and dropping the conflicting earlier one
Tailwind classes are applied in alphabetical order automatically, so renaming the classes fixes the conflict
This is a bug in Tailwind's JIT compiler that was fixed in later versions and requires only an upgrade
className props are ignored by Tailwind components unless wrapped in a css-in-js styled() call
explanation: p-4 and p-2 don't collide by class name, so both remain in the class list; because they set the same underlying property, CSS resolves the tie by source order in the generated stylesheet, not by which class appears 'later' in your JSX. tailwind-merge is purpose-built to detect same-property utility conflicts and keep only the intended one.

promptText: A team ships a themeable component library using CSS custom properties with `var(--brand-color, #2563eb)` as a fallback. A consuming app defines `--brand-color: not-a-color;` by mistake. What happens?
options: The fallback does NOT apply, because var() fallbacks only trigger when the property is genuinely unset, not when it holds an invalid value for that context; the invalid value instead resets to the property's inherited or initial value per CSS's invalid-at-computed-value-time behavior
The fallback #2563eb is used automatically, since var() fallbacks catch any value the browser cannot successfully apply
The build fails at compile time because CSS custom properties are type-checked against their declared fallback type
The browser throws a runtime JavaScript error that must be caught with an error boundary
explanation: The var() fallback is specifically for the 'never defined anywhere in the cascade' case. If --brand-color IS defined but holds a nonsensical value for the property using it, that's a different situation -- CSS's invalid-at-computed-value-time rule resets the property to its inherited or initial value, not the var() fallback, which is a commonly missed distinction even among experienced engineers.

promptText: A large app has a decade-old global stylesheet with an `#legacy-header .nav a { color: red !important; }` rule from a long-forgotten fix. New feature work now needs a more specific, semantically-correct override and keeps having to add its own `!important` and ID hacks to win. Using cascade layers (`@layer`), how would a senior engineer resolve this without escalating specificity further?
options: Wrap the legacy stylesheet's rules in an early, low-priority named layer (e.g. `@layer legacy`) declared before the layers used for new components; any rule in a later-declared layer wins over anything in an earlier layer regardless of selector specificity or !important weight within normal (non-important) declarations
Delete the legacy rule outright without wrapping it in anything, since @layer cannot interact with existing un-migrated CSS at all
Add an even higher-specificity ID selector plus !important to the new rule, since @layer only affects unscoped utility classes
Rename the legacy class so the old selector no longer matches any element in the DOM
explanation: Cascade layers let precedence be decided by layer declaration order rather than specificity, so a low-specificity rule in a later-declared layer beats a high-specificity ID + !important rule sitting in an earlier layer (important declarations still invert this ordering, but for normal declarations layer order dominates specificity). Containing legacy CSS in its own early layer lets new, low-specificity component styles reliably win without an escalating specificity war -- note unlayered CSS still beats any layered CSS, so the legacy rule must actually be wrapped in a layer for this to work.

promptText: A Next.js marketing site inlines critical CSS in `<head>` for above-the-fold content and loads the rest of the stylesheet asynchronously via `<link rel="preload" as="style" onload="this.rel='stylesheet'">`. Why is this pattern preferable to simply making the entire stylesheet non-blocking?
options: Making all CSS non-blocking would let the browser paint unstyled content immediately, causing a Flash of Unstyled Content and a visible jump once styles arrive; the hybrid approach keeps only a small, essential subset in the blocking path for a correct first paint while deferring the rest, which is safe to apply after because it doesn't affect what's already visible
Async CSS loading is not actually supported by any modern browser, so critical CSS extraction is the only working option
Inlining all CSS in the head is always faster than any async pattern, so the split only exists for legacy browser compatibility
The full stylesheet must load synchronously anyway for JavaScript event handlers to attach correctly to styled elements
explanation: CSS blocks render by design to prevent FOUC -- the browser deliberately waits for the CSSOM before painting so the first paint is correct rather than unstyled-then-jumping. Critical CSS extraction keeps that safety for just the above-the-fold subset (paid for as a small inlined cost) while letting the much larger remainder load asynchronously, since applying it later only adds below-the-fold styling rather than changing anything already painted.
